questiontext.text: In mutation testing, a mutant is:

answer.text: A copy of the program with one small syntactic change applied by a mutation operator

feedback.text: Correct — a mutant is the original program seeded with one deliberate, small fault.

answer.text: A test case that exposes a defect in the program

feedback.text: That is a failing test case, not a mutant — the mutant is the altered program.

answer.text: A bug reported by a user in production

feedback.text: Mutants are artificial faults injected on purpose, not field-reported defects.

answer.text: An input value that maximises code coverage

feedback.text: Coverage-maximising inputs are a testing concern, unrelated to what a mutant is.

generalfeedback.text: A mutant is a variant of the program produced by applying a mutation operator that makes one small syntactic change (e.g. + becomes -). Running tests against mutants measures how good the tests are at detecting such faults.

questiontext.text: A mutation operator is:

answer.text: A rule that systematically transforms the program to produce mutants (e.g. replace + with -)

feedback.text: Correct — each operator encodes a class of small syntactic changes.

answer.text: An arithmetic operator such as + or * in the source code

feedback.text: That is an operator in the program; a mutation operator is a rule that changes such tokens.

answer.text: The test oracle that decides pass or fail

feedback.text: The oracle judges outputs; it does not generate mutants.

answer.text: A metric describing how many tests pass

feedback.text: That is closer to a test result, not a mutation operator.

generalfeedback.text: A mutation operator is a transformation rule (ROR, AOR, LOR, statement deletion, etc.) applied to the source to systematically generate mutants, each carrying one small change.

questiontext.text: The primary purpose of mutation testing is to:

answer.text: Measure the fault-detecting adequacy of a test suite

feedback.text: Correct — it asks "how many injected faults do these tests catch?"

answer.text: Automatically repair bugs in the program

feedback.text: Mutation testing evaluates tests; it does not fix code.

answer.text: Prove the program has no defects

feedback.text: No testing technique proves the absence of all defects.

answer.text: Generate program inputs at random

feedback.text: Random input generation is a different technique; mutation testing seeds faults, not inputs.

generalfeedback.text: Mutation testing evaluates how good a test suite is by seeding artificial faults (mutants) and measuring the fraction the suite detects — a stronger adequacy criterion than structural coverage alone.

questiontext.text: A mutant is considered killed when:

answer.text: Some test case produces a different result on the mutant than on the original program

feedback.text: Correct — that observable difference is what "kills" it.

answer.text: The mutant fails to compile

feedback.text: A mutant that won't compile is usually discarded (a stillborn mutant), not "killed" by a test.

answer.text: The mutant crashes at runtime

feedback.text: A crash kills a mutant only if it differs from the original's behaviour — the definition is about differing output, not crashing itself.

answer.text: The mutant is equivalent to the original

feedback.text: An equivalent mutant, by definition, can never be killed by any test.

generalfeedback.text: A mutant is killed when at least one test case in the suite yields an observable difference (output, state, or crash vs. no crash) between running that test on the mutant and on the original program.

questiontext.text: A mutant that lives (survives) against a test suite is one that:

answer.text: Produces the same result as the original on every test in the suite

feedback.text: Correct — no test in the suite distinguishes it, so it survives.

answer.text: Produces a different result on at least one test

feedback.text: That describes a killed mutant, not a surviving one.

answer.text: Cannot be compiled or executed

feedback.text: That is a stillborn mutant, a separate category from live mutants.

answer.text: Is always an equivalent mutant

feedback.text: A live mutant may be equivalent, but it may instead be non-equivalent and simply not yet killed by a weak suite.

generalfeedback.text: A live (surviving) mutant gives the same output as the original on every test in the suite. It signals either a weakness in the tests (a non-equivalent mutant that a better test would kill) or an equivalent mutant that no test can kill.

questiontext.text: An equivalent mutant is a mutant that is:

answer.text: Syntactically different from the original but semantically identical on every input

feedback.text: Correct — same input/output behaviour for all inputs, so no test can distinguish it.

answer.text: Textually identical to the original program

feedback.text: Mutation operators always introduce a syntactic change; identical text isn't a mutant at all.

answer.text: A mutant located in dead/unreachable code

feedback.text: An unreachable mutant fails on reachability, but might still be non-equivalent were the code reached.

answer.text: A mutant that crashes on every input

feedback.text: A mutant that reliably crashes differently from the original is trivially killed, not equivalent.

generalfeedback.text: An equivalent mutant differs in source code from the original but computes exactly the same function — identical output for every possible input — so it is logically impossible for any test to kill it.

questiontext.text: The mutation score is computed as:

answer.text: killed mutants / (total mutants − equivalent mutants)

feedback.text: Correct — equivalent mutants are excluded because no test can ever kill them.

answer.text: killed mutants / total mutants

feedback.text: This treats equivalent mutants as killable, unfairly penalising the test suite.

answer.text: killed mutants / (total mutants + equivalent mutants)

feedback.text: Adding, not subtracting, equivalents makes the score worse without justification.

answer.text: (total mutants − killed mutants) / total mutants

feedback.text: That's closer to a "surviving-mutant rate", not the mutation score.

generalfeedback.text: Mutation score = killed / (total − equivalent). Equivalent mutants are removed from the denominator because, being semantically identical to the original, no test could ever kill them.

questiontext.text: A test suite achieves a mutation score of 100% (with equivalents excluded). This means:

answer.text: Every non-equivalent mutant was killed by some test in the suite

feedback.text: Correct — a perfect score means all killable mutants were detected.

answer.text: The program is proven correct

feedback.text: Killing all mutants shows the tests catch these seeded faults, not that the program is bug-free.

answer.text: There were no equivalent mutants

feedback.text: Equivalent mutants are excluded from the denominator; a 100% score says nothing about how many there were.

answer.text: The suite achieves 100% branch coverage

feedback.text: A high mutation score usually implies strong coverage, but 100% is defined by killed mutants, not branches directly.

generalfeedback.text: A 100% mutation score means the suite killed every non-equivalent mutant. It is a strong adequacy signal but is not a proof of program correctness.

questiontext.text: The competent programmer hypothesis underlying mutation testing states that:

answer.text: Programmers write code that is close to correct, so real faults are small deviations from the correct program

feedback.text: Correct — this justifies modelling faults as small single mutations.

answer.text: Programmers never introduce faults into their code

feedback.text: If that were true there would be nothing to test; the hypothesis is about faults being small, not absent.

answer.text: Every fault requires many simultaneous changes to fix

feedback.text: The hypothesis assumes the opposite — faults are typically small deviations.

answer.text: Compilers can detect all programmer mistakes

feedback.text: That is unrelated; the hypothesis concerns the size of human faults, not compiler capability.

generalfeedback.text: The competent programmer hypothesis says developers produce nearly-correct programs, so faults are small. This justifies using small, single-change mutants to model realistic faults.

questiontext.text: The coupling effect hypothesis claims that:

answer.text: Tests that detect all simple (single-change) faults also detect most complex (multiple-change) faults

feedback.text: Correct — this is why testing against simple mutants is worthwhile.

answer.text: Complex faults are completely independent of simple faults

feedback.text: The coupling effect claims the opposite — complex faults are coupled to simple ones.

answer.text: Two modules that share data must be tested together

feedback.text: That is module coupling in design, not the mutation-testing coupling effect.

answer.text: Every mutant is coupled to exactly one test case

feedback.text: The coupling effect relates simple and complex faults, not mutants to individual tests.

generalfeedback.text: The coupling effect holds that a test set killing all simple one-change mutants will also detect the great majority of complex, higher-order faults — so first-order mutants are a good adequacy target.

questiontext.text: Consider if (x > 0) return "positive"; else return "non-positive";. The operator > → >= gives the mutant if (x >= 0) .... For the test input x = 0, the outcome is:

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: Correct — at x=0 the original returns "non-positive" but the mutant returns "positive".

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: x=0 is exactly the boundary where the two operators disagree, so the test does detect it.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is clearly non-equivalent: x=0 distinguishes it.

generalfeedback.text: At x=0 the original's "x>0" is false (returns "non-positive"), but the mutant's "x>=0" is true (returns "positive"). The outputs differ, so this test kills the mutant.

questiontext.text: Consider return age >= 18;. The operator >= → > gives the mutant return age > 18;. For the test input age = 18, the outcome is:

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: Correct — at age=18 the original returns true but the mutant returns false.

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: age=18 is the boundary where ">=18" and ">18" disagree, so this test does detect it.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is non-equivalent: age=18 distinguishes the two.

generalfeedback.text: At age=18 the original's "age>=18" is true, but the mutant's "age>18" is false. The results differ, so this test kills the mutant.

questiontext.text: Consider if (x < 0) { x = -x; } return x;. Statement deletion removes x = -x;, giving if (x < 0) { } return x;. For the test input x = -5, the outcome is:

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: Correct — the original returns 5 but the mutant returns -5.

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: With x=-5 the deleted statement would have run, so its removal is observable here.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is non-equivalent: any negative input distinguishes it.

generalfeedback.text: At x=-5 the original negates and returns 5, but the mutant's empty if-body leaves x as -5. Different outputs, so this test kills the mutant.

questiontext.text: Consider return a + b;. The operator + → - gives the mutant return a - b;. For the test input a = 3, b = 7, the outcome is:

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: Correct — 3+7=10 but 3-7=-4.

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Because b=7≠0, a+b and a-b differ, so the test does detect the mutant.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is non-equivalent: any b≠0 distinguishes + from -.

generalfeedback.text: Here a+b=10 but a-b=-4; since b≠0 the two differ (by 2b), so this test kills the mutant.

name.text: Live outcome: sign classify at x = 7

questiontext.text: Consider if (x > 0) return "positive"; else return "non-positive"; with the mutant if (x >= 0) ... (operator > → >=). For the test input x = 7, the outcome is:

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Correct — at x=7 both versions return "positive"; only x=0 would reveal the difference.

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: At x=7 both "x>0" and "x>=0" are true, so outputs match — the test does not kill it.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is not equivalent: x=0 kills it; this particular test just happens to miss it.

generalfeedback.text: At x=7 both "x>0" and "x>=0" evaluate to true, so both return "positive" and the mutant survives this test. It is not equivalent, though — x=0 would kill it.

questiontext.text: Which change is an instance of the ROR (Relational Operator Replacement) operator?

answer.text: Replacing a < b with a <= b

feedback.text: Correct — ROR replaces one relational operator with another (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=).

answer.text: Replacing a + b with a - b

feedback.text: That is AOR (arithmetic operator replacement), not ROR.

answer.text: Replacing a && b with a || b

feedback.text: That is LOR/COR (logical/conditional operator replacement).

answer.text: Deleting the statement a = b;

feedback.text: That is SDL (statement deletion).

generalfeedback.text: ROR replaces a relational operator with each of the other relational operators (and sometimes with true/false), e.g. < becomes <=, >, >=, ==, or !=.

questiontext.text: The AOR (Arithmetic Operator Replacement) operator would transform x * y into which of the following?

answer.text: x + y

feedback.text: Correct — AOR swaps one binary arithmetic operator for another (+, -, *, /, %).

answer.text: x > y

feedback.text: Turning arithmetic into a relation is ROR-style, not AOR.

answer.text: x && y

feedback.text: That introduces a logical operator (LOR), not an arithmetic one.

answer.text: -x * y

feedback.text: Inserting a unary minus is UOI, not AOR.

generalfeedback.text: AOR replaces one binary arithmetic operator with another from {+, -, *, /, %}, e.g. * becomes +.

questiontext.text: The LOR / conditional operator replacement operator applied to a && b most directly produces:

answer.text: a || b

feedback.text: Correct — it replaces one logical connective with another.

answer.text: a == b

feedback.text: That is a relational operator (ROR), not a logical connective.

answer.text: a + b

feedback.text: That is arithmetic (AOR).

answer.text: !a && b

feedback.text: Inserting a negation is UOI; LOR replaces the connective itself.

generalfeedback.text: LOR (logical/conditional operator replacement) swaps one logical connective for another, e.g. && becomes ||.

questiontext.text: The ABS (Absolute Value Insertion) operator mutates an arithmetic expression e into which family of variants?

answer.text: abs(e), -abs(e), and a fail-on-zero variant

feedback.text: Correct — ABS forces e to be tested as non-negative, non-positive, and zero.

answer.text: e + 1 and e - 1

feedback.text: Off-by-one tweaks are not ABS; ABS is about the sign/zero of the expression.

answer.text: e > 0 and e < 0

feedback.text: Those are relational tests, not the ABS value-insertion family.

answer.text: e replaced by a constant literal

feedback.text: Constant replacement is a different operator; ABS wraps e in absolute-value forms.

generalfeedback.text: ABS replaces an expression e with abs(e), -abs(e), and failOnZero(e), forcing tests that exercise e as positive, negative, and zero.

questiontext.text: Which change is an example of the UOI (Unary Operator Insertion) operator?

answer.text: Replacing return x; with return -x;

feedback.text: Correct — UOI inserts a unary operator (here arithmetic negation).

answer.text: Replacing x + y with x - y

feedback.text: That swaps a binary operator (AOR), not inserts a unary one.

answer.text: Replacing x < y with x > y

feedback.text: That is ROR.

answer.text: Deleting x = 0;

feedback.text: That is statement deletion (SDL).

generalfeedback.text: UOI inserts a unary operator into an expression, e.g. x becomes -x, or a boolean b becomes !b, or x becomes ++x.

questiontext.text: The SDL (Statement Deletion) operator produces a mutant by:

answer.text: Removing a single statement from the program

feedback.text: Correct — SDL deletes one statement to check whether any test relies on its effect.

answer.text: Replacing a variable reference with a constant

feedback.text: That is a constant/variable replacement operator, not SDL.

answer.text: Swapping two adjacent statements

feedback.text: Reordering is a different mutation; SDL removes a statement.

answer.text: Negating a boolean condition

feedback.text: That is closer to UOI/COR; SDL deletes rather than negates.

generalfeedback.text: SDL deletes one statement (often replacing it with a no-op). If no test detects the deletion, that statement's effect is untested.

questiontext.text: Under the Reachability–Infection–Propagation (RIP) model, which condition has failed if the mutated statement executes but the program's state is never different afterward?

answer.text: Infection

feedback.text: Correct — reachability held (the statement ran) but the mutation never corrupted the state.

answer.text: Reachability

feedback.text: Reachability already succeeded since the statement executed.

answer.text: Propagation

feedback.text: Propagation only matters once the state has actually been infected; here it never was.

answer.text: The oracle

feedback.text: The RIP model doesn't include an "oracle" condition — oracle problems live in the test-verification step.

generalfeedback.text: RIP requires the mutated statement to be Reached, to Infect the program state (make it differ from the original), and for that infected state to Propagate to the output. Execution without any state difference means infection failed.

questiontext.text: A test suite that achieves 100% statement coverage is guaranteed to kill every non-equivalent mutant.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Statement coverage only guarantees reachability, not that the mutation infects the state or that the infection propagates to an observable output.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — statement coverage guarantees the mutated statement executes (reachability), but says nothing about infection or propagation, so non-equivalent mutants can still survive.

generalfeedback.text: 100% statement coverage satisfies only the "Reachability" leg of the RIP model. A mutant can still survive if infection never occurs or the infected state never propagates to a checked output — so full statement coverage does not guarantee killing every non-equivalent mutant.

questiontext.text: In the Reachability–Infection–Propagation model, which term names the condition that the corrupted state must reach and change the program's observable output? (one word)

answer.text: propagation

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: propagat*

feedback.text: Correct.

generalfeedback.text: Propagation is the third RIP condition: the infected (corrupted) state must flow forward through execution until it changes something the test oracle actually observes.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes weak mutation from strong mutation?

answer.text: Weak mutation checks for a state difference right after the mutated component executes; strong mutation requires the difference to propagate to the program output

feedback.text: Correct — weak mutation only needs infection; strong mutation needs infection to propagate.

answer.text: Weak mutation uses fewer mutation operators than strong mutation

feedback.text: The distinction is about where the difference is observed, not how many operators are used.

answer.text: Weak mutation only applies to equivalent mutants

feedback.text: Both apply to ordinary mutants; the difference is the point of comparison.

answer.text: Strong mutation runs faster because it stops at the mutated statement

feedback.text: It is weak mutation that can stop early at the component; strong mutation runs to output.

generalfeedback.text: Weak mutation compares internal state immediately after the mutated component (reachability + infection). Strong mutation requires the infected state to propagate all the way to the observable output (reachability + infection + propagation).

questiontext.text: A program has 30 mutants; 6 of them are equivalent, and the test suite kills 21. What is the mutation score?

feedback.text: That is 21/30 — it wrongly counts equivalent mutants in the denominator.
That is 21/(30+6) — equivalents must be subtracted, not added.
That is the surviving-mutant rate 9/30, not the mutation score.

generalfeedback.text: Mutation score = killed / (total − equivalent) = 21 / (30 − 6) = 21/24 = 87.5%.

questiontext.text: Selective mutation reduces cost by:

answer.text: Using only a small, carefully chosen subset of mutation operators that still yields nearly the same adequacy

feedback.text: Correct — a few key operators approximate testing with the full set.

answer.text: Testing only the mutants that happen to be equivalent

feedback.text: Equivalent mutants can never be killed, so testing them alone is pointless.

answer.text: Selecting only the test cases that already pass

feedback.text: Selective mutation reduces operators, not tests, and does not filter by pass/fail.

answer.text: Running each mutant against exactly one test

feedback.text: That would weaken detection; selective mutation instead prunes the operator set.

generalfeedback.text: Selective mutation applies only a small subset of operators (e.g. the "sufficient" set) that empirically produces almost the same mutation score as the full operator set, greatly cutting the number of mutants.

name.text: Kill outcome: && to || with differing operands

questiontext.text: Consider return (age >= 18) && citizen; with the mutant return (age >= 18) || citizen; (operator && → ||). For the test input age = 30, citizen = false, the outcome is:

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: Correct — here the two operands differ in truth value (true and false), so AND and OR disagree.

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: AND gives false while OR gives true here, so the test does detect the difference.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: && and || are not equivalent whenever the operands differ, as they do here.

generalfeedback.text: With age=30 (so age>=18 is true) and citizen=false, the original computes true && false = false, but the mutant computes true || false = true. The outputs differ, so this test kills the mutant.

name.text: Live outcome: && to || with equal operands

questiontext.text: Consider return (age >= 18) && citizen; with the mutant return (age >= 18) || citizen; (operator && → ||). For the test input age = 30, citizen = true, the outcome is:

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Correct — both operands are true, so AND and OR both yield true; a test with differing operands would kill it.

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: true && true and true || true both equal true, so the outputs match here.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is not equivalent: age=30, citizen=false would kill it.

generalfeedback.text: With both operands true, true && true = true and true || true = true, so the mutant survives this test. It is not equivalent — an input where the operands differ (e.g. citizen=false) would kill it.

questiontext.text: Consider return a + b; with the mutant return a - b; (operator + → -). For the test input a = 9, b = 0, the outcome is:

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Correct — a+0 and a-0 are both 9, so this test misses the mutant; any b≠0 would kill it.

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: With b=0, a+b and a-b are equal (both 9), so the outputs match — no kill.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is not equivalent: any b≠0 makes + and - differ, killing it.

generalfeedback.text: At b=0, a+b = a-b = 9, so the mutant survives this particular test. It is not equivalent, though: any test with b≠0 (where a+b and a-b differ by 2b) would kill it. This shows a poorly-chosen test input can let a killable mutant live.

name.text: Why equivalent mutants cannot be killed

questiontext.text: Why is it impossible for any test case to kill an equivalent mutant?

answer.text: It computes the same function as the original, so no input can ever make their outputs differ

feedback.text: Correct — killing requires an observable output difference, which an equivalent mutant can never produce.

answer.text: Its mutated statement is always unreachable

feedback.text: Equivalence is about identical behaviour, not reachability; the statement may well execute.

answer.text: It always throws an exception before returning

feedback.text: An exception that differs from the original would actually kill it; equivalence means no difference at all.

answer.text: Test tools automatically skip it

feedback.text: Tools cannot even reliably detect equivalence; the impossibility is inherent, not a tool choice.

generalfeedback.text: A mutant is killed only when some test yields a different observable result from the original. An equivalent mutant computes exactly the same function for every input, so that difference can never arise — no test can kill it.

questiontext.text: Consider int unused = x * 2; return x * x;. Statement deletion removes int unused = x * 2;, giving return x * x;. The outcome is:

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: Correct — unused is written but never read and x * 2 has no side effects, so deleting it cannot change any output.

answer.text: Killed — some test detects it

feedback.text: No test can detect it: the return value x * x is unaffected by the deleted dead store.

answer.text: Lives on this test but a better test would kill it

feedback.text: No input exists that could kill it, so it is equivalent, not merely surviving.

generalfeedback.text: unused is assigned but never read, and x * 2 has no side effects, so deleting that statement cannot change the value returned for ANY x. The mutant is equivalent.

name.text: Equivalent: relational op on a length

questiontext.text: Given n = arr.length (so n >= 0 always), consider if (n > -1) return true; else return false;. The operator > → >= gives if (n >= -1) .... The outcome is:

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: Correct — for every reachable n (n≥0), both "n>-1" and "n>=-1" are true, so the versions never disagree.

answer.text: Killed — some test detects it

feedback.text: The two conditions differ only at n = -1, which an array length can never take, so no test kills it.

answer.text: Lives on this test but a better test would kill it

feedback.text: There is no reachable input that distinguishes them, so it is equivalent, not merely surviving.

generalfeedback.text: "n>-1" and "n>=-1" differ only at n = -1. Because n is an array length (n≥0 by construction), that value is unreachable, so the two versions agree on every possible input — the mutant is equivalent.

questiontext.text: Here n is a list length (so n >= 0). Consider for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i]; mutated by < → != to for (int i = 0; i != n; i++) sum += a[i];. This mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — i increases from 0 and reaches n exactly, so i!=n stops at the same iteration as i<n for every n≥0

feedback.text: Correct — the two loop conditions terminate identically for all non-negative n.

answer.text: Killed by any test with n > 0

feedback.text: For n>0 both loops run exactly n times, producing the same sum, so such a test does not kill it.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because i != n may skip the last element

feedback.text: It does not: i takes 0,1,…,n-1 and then equals n, ending the loop at the same point as i<n.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because the loop never terminates

feedback.text: Since i increments by 1 from 0 and n≥0, i eventually equals n and the loop terminates.

generalfeedback.text: Because i starts at 0 and increments by 1, it hits n exactly; for any n≥0, "i!=n" becomes false at the same iteration "i<n" does. The behaviours are identical on every reachable input, so this is an equivalent mutant. (It would differ only if n could be negative — impossible for a length.)

questiontext.text: Consider int y = x * 2; return (y > 0) ? 1 : 0; mutated by * → + to int y = x + 2; .... For the test input x = 5, the mutated statement runs and y differs (10 vs 7), yet both return 1. Which RIP condition failed on this test?

answer.text: Propagation — the infected state (y) did not change the observable output

feedback.text: Correct — y was infected (10 vs 7), but since both are > 0 the output stays 1, so infection did not propagate.

answer.text: Reachability — the mutated statement never executed

feedback.text: It did execute; y was computed, so reachability held.

answer.text: Infection — the state was never corrupted

feedback.text: Infection did occur: y was 10 in the original and 7 in the mutant.

answer.text: The mutant is equivalent

feedback.text: It is not equivalent — x=-1 or x=0 makes the outputs differ (0 vs 1), killing it.

generalfeedback.text: At x=5, reachability and infection both hold (y = 10 vs 7), but both values are positive so the ternary returns 1 in each version — the difference does not propagate to the output. A test like x=0 (0 vs 2, giving outputs 0 vs 1) would propagate and kill the mutant.

name.text: Weak vs strong: distinguishing a mutant

questiontext.text: Consider int t = x + 1; return t * 0; mutated by + → - to int t = x - 1; return t * 0;. How do weak and strong mutation classify this mutant?

answer.text: Killable under weak mutation (t is infected) but equivalent under strong mutation (the output is always 0)

feedback.text: Correct — t differs immediately after the mutated statement, but t * 0 is 0 for every x, so no output difference ever propagates.

answer.text: Killable under both weak and strong mutation

feedback.text: Strong mutation compares outputs, and the output is always 0, so it cannot be killed strongly.

answer.text: Equivalent under both weak and strong mutation

feedback.text: Weak mutation compares state at t, which does differ (x+1 vs x-1), so it is killable weakly.

answer.text: Killable under strong mutation but equivalent under weak mutation

feedback.text: This is backwards: infection happens at t (weak kill), but the output never differs (strong equivalent).

generalfeedback.text: Weak mutation checks the state right after the mutated component: t is x+1 vs x-1, so it is infected and can be killed weakly. Strong mutation checks the output: t * 0 = 0 for every x, so no test can produce an output difference — strongly, the mutant is equivalent. The same mutant can thus be "killed" weakly yet be equivalent strongly.

questiontext.text: The PIE (Propagation, Infection, Execution) model relates to the RIP model how?

answer.text: They describe the same three conditions — Execution/Reachability, Infection, and Propagation must all hold to reveal a fault

feedback.text: Correct — PIE and RIP name the same necessary conditions for a fault to be observed.

answer.text: PIE adds a fourth condition absent from RIP

feedback.text: Both models use the same three conditions; only the naming/order differs.

answer.text: PIE applies only to equivalent mutants

feedback.text: PIE describes when any fault is revealed, not specifically equivalent mutants.

answer.text: PIE replaces propagation with an oracle-strength condition

feedback.text: Propagation is retained; PIE is just RIP with Execution named for Reachability.

generalfeedback.text: PIE (Propagation–Infection–Execution) and RIP (Reachability–Infection–Propagation) are the same idea: the faulty location must be Executed/Reached, must Infect the state, and that infection must Propagate to an observable output.

questiontext.text: If a test set kills every mutant produced by the statement-deletion (SDL) operator on a program, what structural criterion must that test set at least satisfy?

answer.text: Statement (node) coverage — each statement must be executed, since deleting it is detected

feedback.text: Correct — a deletion can only be detected if the statement runs, so every statement is covered (and its effect observed).

answer.text: Complete path coverage

feedback.text: Killing SDL mutants does not require touring every path; complete path coverage is far stronger.

answer.text: All-DU-paths coverage

feedback.text: SDL relates to executing statements, not to touring every def-use path.

answer.text: No coverage criterion is implied

feedback.text: Detecting a statement's deletion necessarily requires executing that statement.

generalfeedback.text: To kill a statement-deletion mutant, a test must execute the statement (else the deletion is invisible) and observe its effect. Killing all such mutants therefore implies at least statement coverage — one sense in which mutation adequacy subsumes structural coverage.

questiontext.text: In the theory of minimal/dominator mutants, a mutant M1 dominates M2 (for a program) when:

answer.text: Every test that kills M1 also kills M2, so covering M1 makes M2 redundant

feedback.text: Correct — dominated mutants add no new test requirements once the dominator is killed.

answer.text: M1 and M2 are killed by exactly the same single test only

feedback.text: Domination is about set inclusion of killing tests, not a unique shared test.

answer.text: M1 is equivalent and M2 is not

feedback.text: Domination concerns killing-test sets among non-equivalent mutants, not equivalence.

answer.text: M1 has more mutated statements than M2

feedback.text: Domination is about which tests kill them, not how many changes each contains.

generalfeedback.text: A minimal (dominator) mutant set keeps only mutants that are not dominated: M1 dominates M2 if the set of tests killing M1 is a subset of those killing M2, making M2 redundant. Reporting a mutation score over the dominator set avoids inflation from many easy, redundant mutants.

questiontext.text: A program has 40 mutants. The suite kills 18; of the 22 survivors, 4 are later confirmed equivalent. What is the mutation score (equivalents excluded)?

feedback.text: That is 18/40 — the naive score that wrongly counts the 4 equivalents as killable.
That is 18/(40+4) — equivalents must be subtracted, not added.
That is the survivor rate 22/40, not the mutation score.

generalfeedback.text: Excluding equivalents, mutation score = killed / (total − equivalent) = 18 / (40 − 4) = 18/36 = 50%. Confirming equivalents raises the score from the naive 45% because unkillable mutants leave the denominator.

questiontext.text: A higher-order mutant is one that:

answer.text: Contains two or more mutation operators applied together

feedback.text: Correct — first-order mutants have one change; higher-order mutants combine several.

answer.text: Is generated by a higher-priority operator

feedback.text: Order refers to the number of seeded changes, not operator priority.

answer.text: Is always equivalent to the original

feedback.text: Higher-order mutants are usually non-equivalent; some are "subtle" but not by definition equivalent.

answer.text: Can only be killed by higher-order test cases

feedback.text: There is no such thing as a higher-order test case; ordinary tests kill them.

generalfeedback.text: A higher-order mutant applies two or more changes at once. Some combine to form "subtle" faults harder to kill than their constituent first-order mutants, which is why higher-order mutation is studied despite the coupling effect.

questiontext.text: Determining whether an arbitrary mutant is equivalent to the original program is, in general, undecidable.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — deciding functional equivalence of two programs reduces from undecidable problems, so no algorithm solves it in general.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Equivalence of arbitrary programs is undecidable; that is why equivalent mutants must usually be judged by hand or approximated heuristically.

generalfeedback.text: Detecting equivalent mutants means deciding whether two programs compute the same function, which is undecidable in general. In practice teams use heuristics (e.g. compiler-optimisation or constraint-based checks) and manual analysis, and the equivalent-mutant problem is a major cost of mutation testing.

questiontext.text: A suite kills 100% of the non-equivalent mutants. Which conclusion is justified?

answer.text: The suite is adequate with respect to this operator set, but the program may still contain faults no operator modelled

feedback.text: Correct — mutation adequacy is relative to the mutants generated, not a proof of correctness.

answer.text: The program is proven free of all defects

feedback.text: Mutation testing evaluates tests against seeded faults; it cannot prove global correctness.

answer.text: Every possible mutant, including higher-order ones, is killed

feedback.text: A 100% first-order score says nothing certain about untested higher-order mutants.

answer.text: The suite must also have 100% path coverage

feedback.text: High mutation scores correlate with coverage but do not guarantee complete path coverage.

generalfeedback.text: A perfect mutation score means the tests detect every fault the chosen operators can seed — strong evidence of adequacy, but faults outside the operator set (or in the specification) can remain. Mutation adequacy is always relative to the operators used.

questiontext.text: Consider if (x > 0) return "positive"; else return "non-positive"; with the mutant if (x >= 0) ... (operator > → >=). For the test input x = -3, the outcome is:

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Correct — at x=-3 both "x>0" and "x>=0" are false, so both return "non-positive"; only x=0 reveals the difference.

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: At x=-3 both conditions are false, so both versions return "non-positive" — no difference.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is not equivalent: x=0 kills it; this test merely misses it.

generalfeedback.text: At x=-3, "x>0" and "x>=0" are both false, so both versions return "non-positive" and the mutant survives this test. The single killing input is x=0, so the mutant is non-equivalent — a reminder that reaching the boundary matters.

name.text: Live: && to || with both operands false

questiontext.text: Consider return (age >= 18) && citizen; with the mutant return (age >= 18) || citizen; (operator && → ||). For the test input age = 10, citizen = false, the outcome is:

answer.text: Lives — the test does not detect it, though another input would

feedback.text: Correct — both operands are false, so AND and OR both yield false; the mutant survives this test.

answer.text: Killed — the test detects the mutant (its output differs from the original)

feedback.text: false && false and false || false are both false, so the outputs match here.

answer.text: Equivalent — no test input could ever detect the mutant

feedback.text: The mutant is not equivalent: e.g. age=30, citizen=false (true vs false operands) would kill it.

generalfeedback.text: With age=10 (age>=18 is false) and citizen=false, the original computes false && false = false and the mutant false || false = false — identical, so it survives. && and || agree exactly when both operands share a truth value; an input where they differ would kill this non-equivalent mutant.
